did_you_know.text: Hosea presents Israel as a son: the LORD loved him and called him out of Egypt. The Exodus is thus described not only as a national event, but also as an expression of the bond between a father and his son.
Despite the LORD’s calls, Israel turned to worship the Baals and idols. The verse emphasizes the contrast between the LORD’s call and the people’s response.
The LORD describes how he taught Ephraim to walk, carried him in his arms, and healed him. Yet Israel did not recognize that the LORD was the source of his care and salvation.
The LORD describes his guidance of Israel through “human cords” and “bonds of love”—images that emphasize a humane, gentle, and loving relationship, rather than mere coercion.

Israel will not return to Egypt, but neither will he return to the LORD; instead, Assyria will become his king. The verse presents Assyria as the destination toward which Israel turns because he refuses to return.

The sword in Israel’s cities is described as the result of his ways and plans. The devastation is presented not merely as an external threat, but also as the consequence of the people’s political and spiritual conduct.

The verse mentions Ephraim, Israel, Admah, and Zeboiim. The comparison with Admah and Zeboiim expresses the seriousness of the danger, yet the LORD’s heart is changed within him and his compassion is stirred.
The LORD says, “For I am God and not a human being.” This emphasizes that his decision not to destroy Ephraim arises from divine compassion, which differs from human vengeance.
Israel’s return is described as following the LORD when he roars like a lion. The LORD’s voice awakens the children to fear and movement, leading them to draw near to him.
The children will return from Egypt and Assyria like frightened birds and like a dove. The chapter ends with the promise that the LORD will settle them again in their homes.
